docs.title: PME-toolkit
docs.text:
PME-toolkit is a framework for design-space dimensionality reduction in parametric shape optimization, based on:

  • Parametric Model Embedding (PME)
  • Physics-Informed PME (PI-PME)
  • Physics-Driven PME (PD-PME)

The toolkit provides a reproducible, data-driven workflow to construct low-dimensional representations of high-dimensional parametric design spaces while preserving a direct link to the original variables.

Python for daily use. MATLAB for reference validation.

docs.title: Project status
docs.text:
This documentation covers the v1.3.0 APIs in MATLAB and Python, including direct and snapshot eigensolvers and the advanced streamed observation API. Published software versions and archives are available through:

  • PyPI package (installable)
  • Zenodo archive (versioned, citable)
  • GitHub repository
  • GitHub releases

The Python implementation is fully functional and recommended for use. MATLAB remains available as a reference implementation for validation and comparison. The direct/snapshot solvers and streamed APIs require version 1.3.0 or later. See Quickstart for installation and Reproducibility for the validation protocols.

docs.title: What the toolkit does
docs.text:
PME-toolkit enables:

  • reduction of high-dimensional parametric design spaces
  • extraction of dominant modes of variability
  • construction of interpretable latent representations
  • reconstruction of original variables through backmapping
  • reproducible benchmarking across methods and datasets

docs.title: Minimal workflow
docs.text:
A typical PME workflow consists of:

  1. preparing input data (geometry, variables, optional physics)
  2. defining a JSON configuration file
  3. running the dimensionality reduction
  4. analyzing results and visualizations
  5. optionally performing backmapping

docs.title: Reproducibility and benchmarks
docs.text:
PME-toolkit is designed for reproducible benchmarking across methods and datasets.

The repository includes:

  • a tiny self-contained glider case used by the local tests;
  • benchmark configurations for airfoil, underwater glider and propeller data;
  • a complete Zenodo airfoil regression for PME, PI-PME and PD-PME, comparing the preceding implementation and both current languages;
  • controlled streamed experiments up to 1,048,576 observation coordinates.

Standard case workflows are defined through JSON files. The advanced streaming API accepts explicit observation readers, fixed weights and prepared native variables; its reproducible examples include the required reader definitions.

docs.title: Why PME-toolkit?
docs.text:
PME-toolkit extends classical PCA-based approaches through a generalized, weighted formulation tailored to parametric design problems.

  • Analytical backmapping (core feature) Reduced coordinates are mapped analytically to native design variables. Recovering an original training design depends on the retained observation subspace and is not guaranteed after truncation.

  • Generalized formulation with weights PME relies on a weighted POD/PCA formulation, where weights can encode the role of variables (including null weights). The observation metric and paired native-variable components are retained by both direct and snapshot solutions.

  • A shared fitting workflow solver="auto" chooses between the direct observation covariance and the snapshot Gram matrix. Both use the same preprocessing, metric, numerical-rank policy and downstream model interface. See Snapshot formulation.

  • Design-aware latent space Unlike standard PCA (typically applied to state snapshots without variables), PME explicitly incorporates parametric design variables into the embedding.

  • Physics-aware variants PI-PME and PD-PME embed physical information into the dimensionality-reduction process.

Result: interpretable and optimization-ready reduced spaces.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• Embedding → projection of the design space into a reduced latent space
  • Modes → principal directions of variability
  • Retained variance → fraction of variance captured by the reduced space
  • Backmapping → reconstruction of original variables from reduced coordinates

docs.title: Philosophy
docs.text:
PME-toolkit is designed to support:

  • reproducible research
  • transparent dimensionality reduction workflows
  • systematic comparison between methods
  • integration with optimization pipelines

The standard toolkit workflow follows a configuration-driven approach, with explicit datasets, preprocessing settings and solver choices.

docs.title: Citation
docs.text: If you use PME-toolkit in your work, please cite the associated publication (see the Citation page).

docs.title: Backmapping
docs.text: Backmapping reconstructs original design variables from reduced coordinates using a previously computed PME model.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Backmapping maps a point in the reduced space:

x ∈ R^N

to an approximation of the original design variables:

u ≈ u_hat

This enables:

  • interpretation of latent variables
  • reconstruction of physical configurations
  • integration with optimization workflows

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Backmapping requires:

  • a trained embedding model (from a previous PME run)
  • a normalized reduced-coordinate vector in [0,1]^N for the standalone runner
  • the original configuration file used to build the model

The case must have been run with model saving enabled. The saved format is model.npz for Python and model.mat for MATLAB. The fitting solver is already encoded in the model and is not selected again during backmapping.

docs.title: Python
docs.text: pme-back case_back.json

docs.title: MATLAB
docs.text: run_back("case_back.json")

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Backmapping is defined through a dedicated JSON file.

See:

  • Backmapping configuration

for the complete specification.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
The reduced coordinates are provided through an external file (e.g. .txt):

  • each call processes one normalized vector x01
  • its length must equal reduced_space.nconf, or the full retained dimension when that field is omitted

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Backmapping produces:

  • reconstructed design variables
  • optionally formatted outputs for downstream use

Output format and layout are defined in the configuration file.

docs.title: Denormalization
docs.text:
The standalone workflow first maps x01 to physical reduced coordinates alpha, then applies the native rows of the saved basis and restores the original variable scaling. The analytical map is available with either fitting solver; truncation can prevent exact recovery of a particular training design.

This depends on:

  • dataset statistics
  • selected denormalization rule (e.g. "3sigma")

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• dimensionality of x must match the retained modes
  • values should lie within the training domain
  • extrapolation may produce non-physical or invalid configurations
  • results depend on the quality of the original embedding

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Backmapping is a post-processing step that closes the PME workflow by linking reduced representations back to interpretable design variables.

docs.title: Backmapping configuration
docs.text:
Backmapping is defined through a dedicated JSON file with the following structure:

{
  "case_json": "case.json",
  "input": {
    "file": "x01.txt",
    "format": "txt"
  },
  "reduced_space": {
    "nconf": 5
  },
  "denorm": {
    "rule": "3sigma",
    "c": 3.0
  },
  "output": {
    "file": "results/u_base.txt",
    "format": "txt",
    "layout": "col",
    "what": "Ubase",
    "write_meta": true
  }
}

docs.title: case_json
docs.text:
Type: string

Path to the original configuration file used to generate the model. It is resolved relative to the backmapping JSON file. Paths under input, output and the optional run_case.model_file are instead resolved relative to the referenced fitting case directory.

This is required to:

  • reconstruct normalization settings
  • recover dataset structure

docs.title: Input (input)
docs.text: Defines a single vector of normalized reduced coordinates x01, with every component in [0,1]. The standalone workflow processes one design per call.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
• file (string) Path to the file containing reduced coordinates

  • format (string) Input format (e.g. "txt")

docs.title: Reduced space (reduced_space)
docs.text: Selects how many leading modes of the saved model are used for this backmap.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: • nconf (int) Number of reduced coordinates, between one and the model's retained dimension. If omitted, all retained modes are used. The input vector must have exactly this many entries; this field is not a sample count.

docs.title: Denormalization (denorm)
docs.text: Controls how reduced variables are mapped back.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
• rule (string)

    "3sigma" → map each normalized coordinate to [-c*sqrt(lambda), +c*sqrt(lambda)]

    "minmax" → map to that reduced coordinate's observed training range

  • c (float)

    scaling coefficient (typically 3.0)

docs.title: Output (output)
docs.text: Defines output file and format.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
• file (string) Output file path

  • format (string) Output format (e.g. "txt")

  • layout (string)

    "col" → one CSV column "row" → one CSV row

    Text output always writes one value per line.

  • what (string)

    "Ubase" → full reconstructed design vector in original units, with fixed variables reinserted at their baseline values

    "Uact" → active reconstructed variables in original units

    "P" → reconstructed augmented vector in the model's prepared coordinates

    "alpha" → denormalized reduced coordinates

  • write_meta (bool) Write additional metadata

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• the fitting run must first save model.npz (Python) or model.mat (MATLAB)
  • no solver field is required here: backmapping uses the saved basis
  • input reduced coordinates must match the selected reduced_space.nconf
  • denormalization depends on the original dataset statistics
  • the backmapping process reconstructs design variables consistent with the training space

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Backmapping is a post-processing step that maps reduced coordinates back to:

  • original design variables
  • physically interpretable configurations

using the model defined in the original case.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
The repository provides benchmark cases for dimensionality reduction workflows based on PME and its variants.

Each benchmark is defined by a configuration file and an associated versioned dataset. The reproducibility protocols identify the cases covered by automated numerical comparisons.

docs.title: Available benchmarks
docs.text:
• glider
  • airfoil
  • propeller (standard PME)

Benchmarks are organized under benchmarks/ by:

  • method family (PME, PI-PME, PD-PME)
  • selection strategy (standard, goal-oriented)
Case family Glider Airfoil Propeller Standard PME Available Available Available Standard PI-PME / PD-PME Available Available — Goal-oriented PI-PME / PD-PME Available Available —

docs.title: Running a benchmark
docs.text: Benchmarks are executed using the standard workflow via a JSON configuration file. The distributed cases explicitly set "solver": "auto". Changing it to "direct" or "snapshot" selects the numerical formulation while preserving the case data, source metric, preprocessing and output workflow. For a solver comparison, keep all other configuration entries unchanged. Cases that omit the field remain valid and use auto.

docs.title: Python
docs.text: pme-run benchmarks/standard/pme/glider/case.json

docs.title: MATLAB
docs.text:
run_pme("benchmarks/standard/pme/glider/case.json")

Running a benchmark produces:

  • reduced coordinates
  • variance analysis
  • reconstruction error metrics
  • visualization outputs
  • trained model

docs.title: Benchmark structure
docs.text:
Each benchmark includes:

  • a configuration file (case.json)
  • references to dataset files
  • method and preprocessing settings
  • output definitions

The configuration file fully defines the experiment.

docs.title: Data dependencies
docs.text:
Benchmarks rely on datasets that may be:

  • included in lightweight form (tests/data/)
  • referenced through metadata (databases/)
  • distributed externally (e.g. Zenodo)

The standard runner downloads and extracts a missing benchmark database when the matching databases/<name>/dataset.json metadata is available. Manual download remains possible; supply the corresponding local paths in the case configuration. Relative paths are resolved from the case directory.

docs.title: Current maturity
docs.text:
• airfoil → pinned dataset record 10.5281/zenodo.18958555; complete PME/PI/PD regression against the preceding solver and across MATLAB and Python is specified in Zenodo regression.
  • glider → pinned dataset record 10.5281/zenodo.18936594; a tiny local fixture and a full Python case workflow are included in testing.
  • propeller → pinned dataset record 10.5281/zenodo.20207996; a standard PME configuration is provided. This does not imply that the full propeller dataset has the same regression coverage as airfoil.

docs.title: Role of benchmarks
docs.text:
Benchmarks provide:

  • validation of dimensionality reduction workflows
  • comparison between PME, PI-PME, and PD-PME
  • reproducible test cases for development and research

They form the basis for systematic evaluation and benchmarking of methods.

docs.title: Configuration specification
docs.text:
PME-toolkit uses JSON configuration files to define dimensionality reduction workflows.

This page documents the actual configuration schema used by the toolkit.

docs.title: Configuration outline
docs.text:
The following outline abbreviates the nested objects. A complete runnable reference configuration is shown at the end of this page.

{
  "mode": "pi",
  "solver": "auto",
  "CI": 0.95,
  "baseline_col": 0,
  "geom": { ... },
  "vars": { ... },
  "phys": { ... },
  "filters": { ... },
  "io": { ... }
}

docs.title: mode
docs.text:
Type: string

Defines the method:

  • "pme" → geometry + variables
  • "pi" → physics-informed PME
  • "pd" → physics-driven PME

docs.title: CI
docs.text:
Type: float, default 0.99.

Confidence index (retained variance), e.g.:

0.95 → 95% retained variance

The valid interval is (0, 1]. Retention is measured against the complete weighted covariance/Gram trace, before numerical rank truncation. If the selected boundary intersects a repeated eigenvalue cluster, the whole cluster is kept. If the resolved spectrum cannot reach the requested CI, all resolved modes are retained and a warning reports the achieved fraction.

docs.title: solver (optional)
docs.text:
Type: string, default "auto".

This field is optional for existing configurations. The distributed fitting examples and benchmarks declare "solver": "auto" explicitly for clarity. An omitted field selects auto; an empty string, null, or an unsupported value is invalid.

  • "auto": solve the smaller symmetric eigenproblem. Use the direct covariance when the number of positive-weight observation rows is smaller than the sample count; use the snapshot Gram otherwise.
  • "direct": explicitly solve the positive-weight observation covariance.
  • "snapshot": explicitly solve the sample-space Gram matrix.

Both formulations use the same fixed weights, positive-rank cutoff, complete eigenvalue clusters, trace-based confidence criterion, and native backmap. The selected solver and its matrix dimension are reported in the model diagnostics. The separate fit_streaming API always uses snapshot assembly.

docs.title: snapshot (optional)
docs.text:
The same numerical options apply to both solvers in MATLAB and Python:

Field Default Meaning eig_rtol S * eps Relative cutoff against the largest eigenvalue, with a minimum of S * eps; S is the number of retained samples and eps is double-precision machine epsilon. eig_atol 0 Absolute eigenvalue cutoff. cluster_rtol 1e-10 Relative gap tolerance for keeping an entire eigenvalue cluster. block_rows 4096 Maximum rows per weighted Gram assembly block.

Eigenvalues must satisfy lambda > max(eig_atol, eig_rtol * lambda_max). Adjacent resolved eigenvalues are treated as one cluster when their gap is at most the larger of that cutoff and cluster_rtol times the larger eigenvalue. Tolerances must be finite and nonnegative; block_rows must be a positive integer. The requested relative cutoff, its effective value after the numerical floor, and achieved retention are stored in the model diagnostics. Setting the requested relative cutoff to zero does not disable the roundoff protection. See Snapshot formulation for storage, numerical limits, and compatibility details.

docs.title: baseline_col
docs.text:
Type: integer

Index of the baseline configuration in the dataset. Indices in JSON files are zero-based: 0 selects the first sample. MATLAB converts JSON indices to its internal one-based convention when reading the case. This also applies to active-variable indices and filter indices.

Used for:

  • normalization
  • fixed-variable handling

docs.title: Geometry (geom)
docs.text: Defines the geometric structure.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
• Jdir (int) Number of spatial directions per point (e.g. 2 → 2D, 3 → 3D)

  • patches (list)

Each patch:

{
  "name": "P1",
  "K": 784
}

Where:

  • name → identifier
  • K → number of points in the patch

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Total geometric dimension:

n_geom = Jdir × sum(K over patches)

docs.title: Variables (vars)
docs.text: Defines parametric design variables.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
• Mbase (int) Total number of variables

  • idx_active (list) Zero-based indices of active variables in the JSON file

    [] → all variables active

  • fixed_policy (string)

    "baseline" → fixed variables set to baseline values

  • Urange_file (string) Path to variable bounds

  • use_db_range_if_missing (bool) Derive ranges from the database when no ranges are supplied (default true). An explicitly named range file must be accessible; remove an unused path rather than naming a nonexistent file.

docs.title: Physics (phys)
docs.text:
Defines physical data used in PI-PME / PD-PME.

For mode: "pi" or mode: "pd", phys must contain at least one entry in fields or scalars. Either source type alone is sufficient. A missing, null, or empty phys block (including two empty source lists) raises a clear configuration error in both MATLAB and Python, before case data is loaded or downloaded. The same validation applies to direct fitting calls.

For portable MATLAB/Python case files, include both fields and scalars lists, leaving any unused list empty. For geometry-only PME, select mode: "pme" and leave both lists empty. Direct fitting calls also accept PME configurations with phys omitted. PI/PD never silently fall back to geometry-only PME.

docs.title: fields
docs.text:
List of distributed fields:

{
  "name": "Cp",
  "nCond": 1,
  "disc": { "K": 784 }
}

Where:

  • name → field name
  • nCond → number of conditions
  • disc.K → discretization size

docs.title: scalars
docs.text:
List of scalar quantities:

{
  "name": "D",
  "nCond": 1
}

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• fields → spatially distributed data
  • scalars → global quantities

docs.title: Filters (filters)
docs.text: Defines dataset filtering.

docs.title: remove_nan (bool)
docs.text: Remove samples containing nonfinite values (NaN or infinity).

docs.title: goal
docs.text:
{
  "enable": true,
  "metrics": [
    {
      "c_offset": 0,
      "rule": "positive"
    }
  ]
}
  • enable → activate filter
  • metrics → list of constraints

Each metric:

  • c_offset → zero-based row offset within the scalar block C
  • rule → filtering rule (e.g. "positive")

docs.title: iqr
docs.text:
{
  "enable": true
}

Apply interquartile range filtering.

docs.title: Input / Output (io)
docs.text: Defines data access and output behavior. Relative dbfile, Urange_file and outdir paths are interpreted from the directory containing the fitting JSON file, not from the current working directory. The standard runner reads the database into memory for every solver.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
• dbfile (string) Path to database file (.mat)

  • transpose_if (string)

    "never" | "always" | "auto"

Controls data orientation. never preserves feature rows and sample columns; always transposes the input; auto uses the configured row count to choose the orientation. The portable MAT database variable names are database and DB.

  • outdir (string) Output directory; defaults to results under the fitting case directory in both languages.

  • save_model (bool) Save the fitted model (model.npz in Python, model.mat in MATLAB). The default is true. Setting false disables model-file writes without deleting an existing model or removing the in-memory result. Set this to true when the subsequent standalone backmapping workflow needs to read that model. Reporting writes report.mat.

docs.title: Backmapping configuration
docs.text: Backmapping has a separate JSON schema beginning with case_json, input, reduced_space, denorm and output. It reads the fitted model and therefore does not need solver or snapshot settings. See Backmapping configuration for the supported fields, coordinate normalization and path rules.

docs.title: Key constraints
docs.text:
• all data must be sample-aligned
  • geometry, variables, and physics must share sample count
  • x dimension must match retained modes
  • paths must be valid and accessible

docs.title: Minimal working example
docs.text:
The following configuration uses the included tiny glider data. Its relative paths assume a file under tests/cases/, as in test_glider.json:

{
  "mode": "pme",
  "solver": "auto",
  "CI": 0.99,
  "baseline_col": 0,
  "geom": {
    "Jdir": 3,
    "patches": [
      { "name": "P1", "K": 784 }
    ]
  },
  "vars": {
    "Mbase": 32,
    "idx_active": [],
    "fixed_policy": "baseline",
    "Urange_file": "../data/glider_range.mat",
    "use_db_range_if_missing": true
  },
  "phys": { "fields": [], "scalars": [] },
  "filters": {
    "remove_nan": true
  },
  "io": {
    "dbfile": "../data/glider_tiny.mat",
    "transpose_if": "never",
    "outdir": "results",
    "save_model": true
  }
}

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The configuration file fully defines:

  • data structure
  • preprocessing
  • method
  • output

and is the central interface of PME-toolkit.

Backmapping uses a separate configuration format (see Backmapping page).

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text: PME-toolkit operates on datasets stored in external files (typically .mat) and referenced through configuration files.

docs.title: Dataset organization
docs.text:
Dataset metadata is documented in:

  • databases/glider/
  • databases/airfoil/
  • databases/propeller/

These folders describe:

  • dataset structure
  • variable definitions
  • required files

docs.title: Benchmark datasets
docs.text: The main benchmark datasets are distributed via Zenodo:

docs.title: Glider
docs.text:
Serani, A., & Palma, G. (2026).
Design-Space Dimensionality Reduction Benchmark Dataset – Bio-Inspired Underwater Glider (1.1) [Data set].
https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18936594

docs.text:
