docs.title: Dataset file
docs.text:
The dataset is specified in the configuration file:

"io": {
    "dbfile": "path/to/database.mat"
}

For a shared MATLAB/Python input, store the feature-by-sample database matrix in a MAT file under database or DB. Variable bounds, when supplied, use an Mbase-by-2 matrix of minima and maxima in range_design or Urange.

The database contains:

  • geometric data
  • design variables
  • optional physical quantities

docs.title: Data structure
docs.text:
Datasets are organized sample-wise, where:

  • each column represents one design configuration
  • all data sources are aligned across samples

The dataset may include:

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
• discretized coordinates
  • structured according to geom definition

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
• parametric design variables
  • dimension defined by vars.Mbase

docs.title: Physics (optional)
docs.text:
• distributed fields (e.g. pressure coefficients)
  • scalar quantities (e.g. drag, lift)

docs.title: Consistency requirements
docs.text:
All dataset components must:

  • have the same number of samples
  • be aligned across geometry, variables, and physics
  • be free of missing values (after filtering)

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
For the supplied benchmark cases, run_case checks for the required files and downloads the archive described by the matching dataset.json when the files are absent. Both language runners use this metadata. The download is unnecessary for the self-contained tiny glider fixture.

To provide a dataset manually:

  1. download the dataset from Zenodo
  2. extract it locally
  3. update the dbfile path in the JSON configuration
  4. run the benchmark

Relative input and output paths are resolved from the directory containing the fitting configuration. Keep the dataset record and source definitions fixed when comparing direct and snapshot. Neither solver choice changes the standard loader into a streaming reader; see the streamed API for observations that cannot be held in memory.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• dataset structure must match the configuration file
  • geometry, variables, and physics must match geom, vars, and phys
  • incorrect alignment will lead to invalid results

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Datasets provide the input to PME workflows and must be:

  • versioned (via Zenodo)
  • structured consistently
  • correctly referenced in configuration files

docs.title: Input data structure
docs.text: PME-toolkit operates on datasets describing the variability of parametric geometries.

docs.title: Data components
docs.text:
A dataset typically includes:

  • geometric data
  • design variables
  • physical quantities (required for PI-PME / PD-PME)

docs.title: Global data matrix
docs.text:
PME-toolkit represents all information through a block-structured data matrix, where each column corresponds to one design realization.

Figure: Structure of the PME data matrix. Geometry, design variables, optional distributed fields, and scalar quantities are stacked into a single matrix. This unified representation enables dimensionality reduction while preserving the link to the original parametric variables.

docs.title: Geometry representation
docs.text:
Geometry is represented as a matrix:

\[ D \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{features}} \times n_{\text{samples}}} \]

Where:

  • n_samples = number of design realizations
  • n_features = number of geometric degrees of freedom

Typical cases:

  • 2D geometry → stacked coordinates
  • 3D geometry → flattened mesh nodes

Within each geometry patch, rows store all point coordinates in the first direction, then the second direction, and then the third when present. Columns remain design samples. Thus a 3D patch with K points contributes 3*K rows; multiple patches follow the order in geom.patches.

docs.title: Design variables
docs.text:
Design variables are stored as:

\[ U \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{variables}} \times n_{\text{samples}}} \]

These correspond to the original parametric model and are explicitly included in the data matrix, enabling analytical backmapping from the reduced space.

docs.title: PME embedding matrix
docs.text:
The fitting matrix depends on mode:

\[ \mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{PME}}=[\mathbf{D};\mathbf{U}],\qquad \mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{PI}}=[\mathbf{D};\mathbf{U};\mathbf{F};\mathbf{C}],\qquad \mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{PD}}=[\mathbf{U};\mathbf{F};\mathbf{C}]. \]

Here U contains the prepared active design variables, F the configured physical fields and C the scalar responses. The input database retains its configured row layout in all three modes; PD-PME excludes geometry when constructing the fitting matrix. Both solvers use the same matrix and metric.

docs.title: Optional physical data
docs.text:
PI-PME and PD-PME require at least one configured physical source, such as:

  • pressure fields
  • performance indicators

Fields and scalars are included in the order specified by phys.fields and phys.scalars. Native rows have zero metric weight but are retained in the recovered modes for analytical backmapping. See Configuration for the required physics declarations and Snapshot formulation for mode recovery.

docs.title: Key requirement
docs.text:
All data must be:

  • aligned sample-wise
  • consistent in dimension
  • free of missing values (after filtering)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The entire PME workflow relies on a consistent data matrix representation, where each column represents one design realization and multiple data sources are combined into a unified embedding space.

docs.title: MATLAB API
docs.text: The MATLAB implementation provides a reference interface for PME-toolkit workflows.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Add the source folder to the MATLAB path:

addpath(genpath("matlab/src"));

docs.title: Running a case
docs.text:
A dimensionality reduction workflow can be executed from a JSON configuration file:

out = pme.run_case("tests/cases/test_glider.json");

docs.title: Backmapping
docs.text:
Backmapping can be performed using a dedicated configuration:

out = pme.backmapping("tests/cases/test_glider_back.json");

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
pme.run_case returns configuration, layout, dataset metadata, original and filtered data, the fitted model, output directory, saved-file paths and report (out.cfg, out.layout, out.meta, out.DB, out.DB_used, out.model, out.outdir, out.saved, out.rep). Model saving writes model.mat; reporting writes report.mat and figures.

For solver diagnostics, inspect out.model.statsW.snapshot, including solver_requested, solver, matrix_dimension, numerical_rank and achieved_ci. The snapshot diagnostic name is shared by both solvers.

pme.backmapping returns out.x01, physical reduced coordinates out.alpha, the reconstructed augmented vector out.P, active variables out.Uact, the requested output vector out.U and out.written_files.

docs.title: Wrappers
docs.text:
Repository-level wrappers are available:

  • run_pme.m
  • run_back.m

These provide a simplified interface to the same JSON-driven workflow:

run_pme("tests/cases/test_glider.json")
run_back("tests/cases/test_glider_back.json")

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: pme.snapshot_decompose(Pc, w, options) exposes the snapshot solver for already centered data with samples in columns. Its result contains resolved eigenvalues, complete modes, training coordinates, sample eigenvectors and diagnostics. pme.weights_diag builds vector weights for the normal fitting path. pme.direct_decompose(Pc, w, options) exposes the equivalent symmetric observation covariance solver. pme.decompose(Pc, w, options, solver) accepts 'auto', 'direct', or 'snapshot'; regular fitting uses cfg.solver with default 'auto'. See Snapshot formulation for numerical options and compatibility with legacy models. An omitted solver field remains valid. JSON indices are zero-based and are converted when reading the case; configurations assembled directly in MATLAB use MATLAB's one-based indices.

docs.title: Row-reader workflow
docs.text:
model = pme.fit_streaming(reader, [Q,S], weights, native, ...
    struct('block_rows',2048), 0.95);
coordinates = pme.transform_streaming(model, reader, query_reader, T, weights);
native_predictions = pme.backmap_streaming(model, coordinates);

Readers return raw observation rows using one-based, inclusive bounds reader(first,last). The metric is a fixed vector or row reader. native is M-by-S, already prepared in the desired native coordinate system. Query coordinates are T-by-N and native predictions are M-by-T. An optional seventh argument, mode_writer(first,last,modes), receives observation modes in a second pass. The default compact model stores no observation matrix or reader handles and can be saved using save. This compact model is separate from the regular pme.run_case model. The standard runner retains the database in memory, even with solver="snapshot".

  • MATLAB and Python implementations follow the same configuration structure
  • JSON files define the full workflow
  • MATLAB is useful for validation and comparison with the reference implementation

docs.title: Python API
docs.text: The Python package provides a working implementation of PME-toolkit, aligned with the MATLAB reference workflow.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
pme-run <case.json>
pme-back <case_back.json>

docs.title: Python usage
docs.text:
from pme_toolkit.run_case import run_case
from pme_toolkit.run_back import run_back

run_case("tests/cases/test_glider.json")
run_back("tests/cases/test_glider_back.json")

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
The Python implementation supports:

  • PME, PI-PME, PD-PME model construction
  • JSON-driven workflows
  • dimensionality reduction and variance analysis
  • backmapping to original variables
  • model persistence (model.npz)
  • direct and snapshot symmetric eigensolvers with automatic selection, vector weights and numerical-rank diagnostics
  • streamed fitting, compact native backmapping and cross-Gram query encoding

The low-level snapshot_decompose(pc, weights, options=None) accepts centered data with samples in columns and returns resolved eigenvalues, complete modes, training coordinates, sample eigenvectors and diagnostics. See Snapshot formulation for conventions and migration of custom code using stored weights. direct_decompose(pc, weights, options=None) has the same outputs; decompose(pc, weights, options=None, solver="auto") selects the smaller symmetric problem. Regular fits accept the same choice in cfg["solver"]. If this setting is omitted, fitting uses auto. The regular model and all downstream APIs are shared by the two solvers. JSON and Python configuration indices are zero-based; baseline_col=0 selects the first input sample.

The positive baseline_col values previously accepted through a MATLAB-style interpretation now follow this same zero-based convention. Custom Python configurations that used one-based indices must subtract one. Existing distributed examples use baseline_col=0 and keep their baseline.

docs.title: Case outputs
docs.text:
run_case returns a dictionary with cfg, layout, meta, case_json, DB, DB_used, model, report, outdir, saved, filter_info and filter_mask. The report is saved as report.mat. With io.save_model=true (the default), model saving writes model.npz and records its path under saved.model_npz. With false, that saved-file entry is absent and the in-memory model remains available. An omitted io.outdir uses results under the fitting case directory. PmeModel.load restores that model for transformation or backmapping.

The effective solver and its diagnostics are available through result["model"].stats_w["snapshot"], including solver_requested, solver, matrix_dimension, numerical_rank and achieved_ci. The snapshot diagnostic name applies to both solvers.

docs.title: Row-reader workflow
docs.text:
from pme_toolkit import fit_streaming, transform_streaming, backmap_streaming

model = fit_streaming(reader, (Q, S), weights, native,
                      {"block_rows": 2048}, ci=0.95)
coordinates = transform_streaming(model, reader, query_reader, T, weights)
native_predictions = backmap_streaming(model, coordinates)

Readers return raw observation rows using zero-based, half-open bounds reader(start, stop). The metric is a fixed vector or row reader. native has shape (M, S) in the already prepared coordinate system chosen by the caller. Query coordinates are (T, N) and native predictions are (M, T). An optional mode_writer(start, stop, modes) receives observation modes in a second pass. See Snapshot formulation for a complete example, provider responsibilities, and storage requirements. The compact streaming model is distinct from PmeModel. The standard run_case workflow retains its database in memory for every solver choice.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
• published package versions are installable via PyPI; the direct/snapshot solvers and streamed APIs require version 1.3.0 or later
  • validated against MATLAB reference through regression tests
  • recommended for standard usage

MATLAB remains the reference for numerical validation.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
This section provides a minimal example to run PME-toolkit and verify that the installation works correctly.

PME-toolkit can be used in two ways:

  • Option A — try a ready-to-run reference case (recommended)
  • Option B — use PME-toolkit on your own data

docs.title: Option A — Run the self-contained reference case
docs.text:
Clone the repository to access ready-to-run benchmark cases:

git clone https://github.com/cnr-inm-mao/pme-toolkit.git
cd pme-toolkit
git switch --detach v1.3.0
python -m pip install -e ./python

The tag selection above installs v1.3.0, including auto, direct, snapshot and streaming. Other released versions are listed on the repository's Releases page.

Run a reference case:

pme-run tests/cases/test_glider.json

Run backmapping:

pme-back tests/cases/test_glider_back.json

docs.title: Option B — Use PME-toolkit on your own data
docs.text:
Install from PyPI:

pip install pme-toolkit

Run PME with your configuration file:

pme-run your_config.json

Run backmapping:

pme-back your_backmapping_config.json

The solvers and streamed APIs require version 1.3.0 or later. Use pip install pme-toolkit==1.3.0 to select this release explicitly. See Input data and Configuration for dataset and variable definitions.

docs.title: MATLAB
docs.text:
Add the source folder to the path:

addpath(genpath("matlab/src"));

Run a reference case:

run_pme("tests/cases/test_glider.json")

Run backmapping:

run_back("tests/cases/test_glider_back.json")

docs.title: What happens
docs.text:
Running the example produces:

  • reduced coordinates
  • variance and mode information
  • reconstruction error metrics
  • output files under tests/cases/results/ for this reference configuration

The saved outputs include report.mat and a model file (model.npz in Python, model.mat in MATLAB), together with diagnostic plots. Backmapping reads the saved model from the preceding run.

docs.title: Solver choice
docs.text:
The reference case and benchmark inputs explicitly include:

"solver": "auto"

This selects the smaller of the direct observation covariance and snapshot Gram problems. Set "direct" or "snapshot" to select a particular solver. Existing fit inputs that omit solver remain valid and default to "auto" in both languages. No solver field is needed in a backmapping configuration. See Solver selection for the numerical contract.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• the dataset under tests/data/ is self-contained and requires no external downloads
  • JSON configuration files define the full workflow
  • ready-to-run examples are available in the repository under tests/cases/
  • for full benchmark workflows, see the Benchmarks and Datasets sections
  • the regular case runner loads the database into memory even when solver="snapshot"; use the row-reader API for streamed observation data

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
PME-toolkit is designed to support reproducible dimensionality reduction workflows through:

  • configuration-driven execution (JSON files)
  • versioned datasets
  • benchmark definitions

docs.title: Self-contained validation
docs.text:
The repository includes a minimal dataset and test cases for quick validation:

  • data: tests/data/
  • configurations: tests/cases/

These provide a small workflow that does not require an external dataset.

docs.title: MATLAB
docs.text: run("tests/matlab/run_tests.m")

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
pytest tests/python -q --ignore=tests/python/test_run_case.py

The excluded integration test uses the complete external glider database. Run pytest tests/python -q to include it; that run can download the benchmark archive. The tiny fixture and the remaining local tests need no external data.

docs.title: Direct and snapshot validation
docs.text:
The snapshot tests compare a controlled spectrum with an independent symmetric observation-covariance calculation. They check weighted orthonormality, complete repeated eigenspaces, zero-weight native components, native reconstruction, rank-deficient inputs, row-block assembly, and variance-based mode selection. The auto, direct and snapshot choices use the same prepared data, metric and numerical tolerances. The direct option is also exercised when the number of observations is smaller than the number of samples.

Both languages also use tests/data/snapshot_parity.json for PME, PI-PME, and PD-PME. It contains the same geometry, native variables, physical fields and scalars, including a constant source. To compare the current implementations:

run("tests/matlab/run_tests.m")
export_snapshot_parity("snapshot_parity.json")

python tests/python/compare_snapshot_parity.py snapshot_parity.json

The MATLAB CI job runs this comparison after its test suite. It checks eigenvalues, selected dimension, weights, sample subspaces, native reconstructions, total variance and achieved retention with explicit tolerances. Modes are compared through invariant quantities, so signs and rotations within repeated eigenspaces do not create false failures.

The complete Python suite includes a benchmark workflow that may download an external dataset. For tests that do not require that download, use:

pytest tests/python -q --ignore=tests/python/test_run_case.py

docs.title: Streamed MATLAB and Python comparison
docs.text:
The fixture tests/data/snapshot_curve.json stores the same native construction and query designs for both languages. The observation reader evaluates the documented nonlinear curve at midpoint locations. The export checks resident direct and snapshot results, optional observation-mode writing, cross-Gram query encoding and a native-only fit with 1,048,576 observation rows:

addpath("matlab/src")
addpath("tests/matlab")
export_streaming_parity("streaming_parity.json")

The MATLAB CI workflow compares the exported results with the current Python implementation. Its comparisons use eigenvalues, selected sample subspaces and native backmaps, accounting for the sign ambiguity of eigenvectors. The large run also verifies that the reader never receives more rows than the configured block size and that one fitting pass reads every row exactly once.

docs.title: Controlled manuscript experiments
docs.text:
Run the toolkit verification driver from the repository root, using the Python package installed from that checkout:

python -m pip install -e ./python
python benchmarks/snapshot/verify_manuscript.py \
  --output benchmarks/results/snapshot_manuscript.json

The driver and the fixed native-input fixture are versioned. The report is a generated local output: benchmarks/results/ is created on demand and excluded from Git. Each run overwrites the requested output file; choose a different --output path to preserve multiple runs.

The driver calls the public direct_decompose, snapshot_decompose, fit_streaming, transform_streaming and backmap_streaming APIs. It performs four experiments:

Experiment Fixed setup Main outputs Prescribed spectrum 160 observations, 48 samples, six native variables; eigenvalues \([4,1,1,0.1,0.01,0.001]\) Positive eigenvalues, complete repeated eigenspaces, native backmaps, orthonormality and residuals Geometric audit 256 observation rows, 64 construction and 128 independent query designs, eight native variables Retained variance, native error, modal error, regenerated-geometry error and domain violations Conditioning Six positive directions spanning 2, 6, 10, 12 and 14 decades Resolved rank, eigenvalue error and native error including any discarded directions Streamed scale 1,048,576 rows, 64 construction samples, eight native variables, six retained modes, blocks of 2048 rows Exact reader-call bounds, construction and query backmaps, elapsed times and process peak resident memory

The geometric observations are

\[ y(t;u)=0.12\sin(\pi t)+ \sum_{j=1}^{8}\frac{0.04}{j^{1.2}}u_j\sin(j\pi t)+ 0.025u_1u_2\sin(9\pi t), \qquad u\in[-1,1]^8. \]

The metric is uniform \(1/Q\). Native designs are fixed in tests/data/snapshot_curve.json: NumPy default_rng(20261020), first a uniform draw of shape (8,64), then one of shape (8,128). The explicit fixture removes any dependence on another language's random generator or array-filling order. The confidence target for the six-mode streamed case is fixed between the five-mode and six-mode cumulative fractions of the 256-row case. The large case has the same discrete inner products for this sine family, providing an independent small resident-data reference for its spectrum and native backmap.

The JSON output records the protocol, source-file SHA256 values, repository revision, whether the working tree was modified, Python and NumPy versions, cutoffs and all measured quantities. It uses one numerical-library thread. The large case runs in a separate process, so peak resident memory includes the interpreter, imported libraries, inputs and temporary arrays without carrying allocations from the preceding experiments. Analytical array sizes are reported separately. Timings are single observations from that environment, not a repeated performance study or measurements of file I/O.

For a release or manuscript reference, run this protocol on the exact source revision being cited, with a clean working tree, and publish the selected report as a release attachment. Preserve its recorded provenance and measurements. Report publication is a separate step from running the driver; routine local outputs should remain unversioned.

Use --skip-large to run only the smaller checks, or --large-rows Q to change the streamed resolution. These arguments are recorded through the output dimensions. The retained spectrum and native reconstructions are compared with explicit tolerances; no historical manuscript numbers are hard-coded as a reference.

The archived reference scripts used by earlier manuscript drafts are not part of these inputs. Sharing a seed does not specify their draw order. Manuscript tables and statements about the implementation must use the measured toolkit outputs and cite their version, rather than relabelling earlier results.

docs.title: Benchmark reproducibility
docs.text:
Full benchmark runs rely on external datasets.

These datasets are:

  • documented under databases/
  • distributed via Zenodo
  • referenced by benchmark configuration files

Run a supplied benchmarks/**/case.json with either case runner. Missing data are obtained from the matching databases/<name>/dataset.json metadata. For a manual download, extract the archive and set the configuration paths relative to its case directory. The examples explicitly set solver="auto"; existing inputs that omit the field still default to that choice. Set direct and snapshot explicitly when comparing their numerical results on the same case.

docs.title: Zenodo regression against the preceding implementation
docs.text:
The Zenodo airfoil regression compares PME, PI-PME and PD-PME on the complete published RAE2822 database with the unchanged implementation at commit 68309805e9aff5a9b877c33982c7181d8faa550b. It checks the dataset hash, uses the existing standard-case sample filters, and does not take a smaller sample subset for the snapshot calculation.

The regression checks explained variance, resolved positive eigenvalues, weighted eigenvectors and native backmaps against both the historical solver and an independent symmetric direct reference. It aligns isolated eigenvectors by sign and compares repeated clusters through their invariant subspaces. Current and historical MATLAB exports can be included in the same report. The linked protocol documents the exact dataset, tolerances, commands and CI artifacts. This full-dataset check is separate from the small unit suite.

docs.title: Configuration-driven workflow
docs.text:
Standard case experiments use JSON configuration files. The controlled streaming experiments use the versioned verification driver and the explicit native-sample fixture described above.

This ensures:

  • reproducibility across environments
  • transparency of preprocessing and methods
  • portability of experiments

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• results depend on dataset version and configuration
  • ensure consistency between dataset and JSON specification
  • benchmark cases provide reference configurations for reproducibility

docs.title: Snapshot formulation
docs.text: Version 1.3.0 provides direct and snapshot symmetric eigensolvers for PME, PI-PME and PD-PME in both MATLAB and Python. The snapshot solver develops the Python implementation contributed by Antoine DeBlois in pull request #1.

docs.title: Solver selection
docs.text:
The case configuration accepts solver:

Value Eigenproblem When it is useful auto (default) Chooses the smaller symmetric problem Normal case workflows snapshot Sample Gram matrix, \(S\times S\) More observation rows than construction samples direct Weighted observation covariance, \(Q_+\times Q_+\) Fewer positive-weight observation rows than construction samples

Here \(Q_+\) counts rows with positive metric weight; native rows do not increase the direct eigenproblem. auto chooses direct when \(Q_+<S\), otherwise snapshot. For a matched numerical comparison, explicitly run both choices on the same data and configuration. The selected solver, requested solver and matrix dimension are recorded under the existing stats_w["snapshot"] / statsW.snapshot diagnostics. The snapshot options object supplies the numerical tolerances for both solvers.

docs.title: One fitting pipeline
docs.text:
Both solvers use the same case loading, filtering, variable preparation, centering and source weights. The solver setting changes the matrix used for the eigensolve and the corresponding mode recovery. The positive-spectrum selection, rank cutoff, trace diagnostics and confidence selection are shared. Both return the same model interface to transformation, native backmapping, reporting and plotting. auto selects one of these two solvers; it does not introduce a third fitting implementation.

There is one direct implementation in the toolkit. It replaces the previous augmented covariance-times-metric eigensolve. The earlier implementation is retrieved from the pinned Git revision only for regression tests; it is not copied into the package or selected by a runtime fallback.

docs.title: Why the direct implementation changed
docs.text:
The previous direct code solved \(CWz=\lambda z\), where \(C=P_cP_c^\mathsf{T}/S\) and \(W=\operatorname{diag}(w)\), on all \(R\) rows, including zero-weight native variables. Although the positive eigenvalues are real, \(CW\) is generally nonsymmetric.

The direct path now solves \(BB^\mathsf{T}/S\), with \(B=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w_+})P_{c,+}\). This symmetric eigenproblem has dimension \(Q_+\) and excludes zero-weight rows. Observation modes are recovered by undoing the positive row scaling; native and other zero-weight components are recovered from the paired sample coefficients. This gives the same resolved positive PME eigenspaces, subject to numerical precision and the usual sign or repeated-eigenspace basis freedom. The symmetric solver supplies an orthonormal observation basis, including within repeated eigenspaces; undoing the row scaling yields metric-orthonormal modes. Normalizing general eigenvectors individually does not by itself enforce this mutual orthogonality.

The change therefore reduces the eigenproblem dimension and uses a symmetric eigensolver with the same spectral policy as snapshot. Diagonal weight storage is a shared improvement used by both solvers. Dense weight-builder interfaces remain thin compatibility wrappers over the single diagonal implementation. These structural savings do not imply a universal reduction in total peak memory or runtime: direct fitting also constructs the weighted observation array and paired sample vectors. The complete-dataset comparison is described in Zenodo regression.

{
  "solver": "auto",
  "snapshot": {
    "eig_rtol": 1e-12,
    "eig_atol": 0,
    "cluster_rtol": 1e-10,
    "block_rows": 2048
  }
}

docs.title: Data and metric
docs.text:
Let \(P_c\) contain the centered construction samples as columns, with \(R\) rows and \(S\) samples. The toolkit keeps its existing row ordering:

  • PME: geometry and active native variables;
  • PI-PME: geometry, active native variables, physical fields and scalars;
  • PD-PME: active native variables, physical fields and scalars.

The vector \(w\) contains the existing variance-normalized observation weights. Native-variable rows have zero weight. The corresponding diagonal matrix is never needed by the fitting path.

docs.title: Gram eigenproblem and lifting
docs.text:
The sample matrix is

\[ K = \frac{1}{S}P_c^\mathsf{T}\operatorname{diag}(w)P_c. \]

Row scaling applies the weights. Contributions are accumulated in blocks of at most snapshot.block_rows rows, using the same fixed weights in every block. The completed matrix is symmetrized before its eigenproblem is solved.

For a unit sample eigenvector \(a_k\) and a resolved positive eigenvalue \(\lambda_k\), the complete mode and construction coordinates are

\[ z_k = \frac{P_c a_k}{\sqrt{S\lambda_k}}, \qquad x_k^\mathsf{T} = \sqrt{S\lambda_k}\,a_k. \]

Lifting uses every data row, including native variables with zero metric weight. The native part of the mode therefore preserves the analytical backmap. No inverse or pseudoinverse of the semidefinite metric is required. For a common retained sample basis \(A\), the centered native reconstruction is \(UAA^\mathsf{T}\). This equals \(U\) only when its row space lies in the retained observation sample space. Keeping every resolved observation mode does not guarantee exact recovery of unrelated native variation.

The existing run_case, transform and backmapping interfaces continue to use the construction means, native scaling and variable bounds. The eigensolver does not enforce bounds on newly chosen reduced coordinates.

docs.title: Numerical rank and retained variance
docs.text:
Only eigenvalues satisfying

\[ \lambda_k > \tau, \qquad \tau = \max(\tau_{\mathrm{abs}},\tau_{\mathrm{rel}}\lambda_1) \]

are lifted. Defaults are eig_atol = 0 and eig_rtol = S * eps. The effective relative cutoff is at least S * eps, even when a smaller value is requested; both values are recorded. This prevents lifting roundoff modes when the configured tolerances are zero. Negative eigenvalues larger than the roundoff allowance cause an error; null or unresolved modes are omitted. A dataset with no resolved positive weighted variance raises an explicit error.

The requested confidence index uses the complete constructed trace:

\[ \rho_N = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{N}\lambda_k}{\operatorname{tr}(K)}. \]

This denominator is not replaced by the sum of the eigenvalues left after thresholding or by the count of information sources. Constant sources still appear in the source metadata but contribute no variance. Mode selection keeps the whole cluster intersecting the confidence threshold. If numerical rank truncation prevents reaching the requested confidence, the fit warns and records the achieved fraction.

The Gram construction squares the positive-spectrum condition number of the weighted data. Small eigenvalues and their native modes can therefore lose accuracy. Diagnostics record the absolute and relative cutoff, numerical rank, cluster tolerance, total variance and achieved retention.

docs.title: Model compatibility
docs.text:
model.W in MATLAB and model.w in Python store a vector of diagonal weights in newly fitted models. When adapting custom code, replace multiplication by the former dense matrix with row scaling. pme.weights and Python build_weights retain their explicit dense return for callers that request it; the normal fit uses the diagonal-only builders. Python loading and MATLAB transform/report functions also accept legacy dense diagonal model weights.

Full-spectrum arrays now contain only resolved positive modes. Their size is the numerical rank, rather than the number of state rows or samples. lam_cum_ninf remains a report compatibility alias for the trace-normalized retained_variance values.

docs.title: Streamed observations and compact native models
docs.text:
The standard case loader keeps the database in memory. For observations stored on disk or generated in blocks, both languages also expose fit_streaming, transform_streaming and backmap_streaming. This path always uses the snapshot eigenproblem and reads at most block_rows observation rows at a time.

The fitting inputs are a repeatable observation reader, the shape \((Q,S)\), fixed effective weights, and paired native data with shape \((M,S)\). The native array is supplied separately; do not append its rows to the observation reader. For PME the reader supplies geometry; for PI-PME it supplies geometry, fields and scalars; for PD-PME it supplies fields and scalars. Row ordering, sample IDs, units and weights must remain identical on every pass.

Weights can be a vector or a reader. They must include any quadrature, source balancing or variance normalization before fitting. A source variance can be accumulated in a preliminary pass over that entire source. Normalizing each storage block independently changes the metric and is not equivalent.

The reader returns raw observations. The fit subtracts construction means rowwise, accumulates the complete Gram matrix, selects complete resolved eigenspaces, and returns the selected sample coefficients, construction coordinates and native modes. It does not retain the observation matrix, its modes, its row means or the readers. Native scaling and active-variable selection are the caller's responsibility in this lower-level interface; backmapping returns the same native units that were supplied, without clipping.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Python readers use zero-based, half-open bounds. A reader backed by a NumPy memory map can be used as follows:

import numpy as np
from pme_toolkit import fit_streaming, transform_streaming, backmap_streaming

observations = np.load("observations.npy", mmap_mode="r")  # Q by S
native = np.load("native.npy")  # M by S, paired construction designs
weights = np.load("weights.npy", mmap_mode="r")  # Q effective weights
reader = lambda start, stop: observations[start:stop, :]

model = fit_streaming(
    reader, observations.shape, weights, native,
    {"block_rows": 2048, "eig_rtol": 1e-12}, ci=0.99,
)
construction_native = backmap_streaming(model, model["coordinates"])

queries = np.load("queries.npy", mmap_mode="r")  # same Q rows, T queries
query_reader = lambda start, stop: queries[start:stop, :]
coordinates = transform_streaming(
    model, reader, query_reader, queries.shape[1], weights,
)
query_native = backmap_streaming(model, coordinates)  # M by T

docs.title: MATLAB
docs.text:
MATLAB readers use one-based, inclusive bounds. With a caller-defined disk or generator reader, the equivalent calls are:

% reader(first,last) returns (last-first+1)-by-S raw observations.
% weights is a Q-vector or weights(first,last) returns matching row weights.
options = struct('block_rows', 2048, 'eig_rtol', 1e-12);
model = pme.fit_streaming(reader, [Q,S], weights, native, options, 0.99);
construction_native = pme.backmap_streaming(model, model.coordinates);
coordinates = pme.transform_streaming(model, reader, query_reader, T, weights);
query_native = pme.backmap_streaming(model, coordinates);  % M by T

Coordinates use one design per row in both implementations. Readers and native inputs use one design per column. The compact model fields have the same names in MATLAB and Python: shape, eigenvalues, sample_vectors, lifting, coordinates, native_mean, native_modes, nconf and info. eigenvalues contains the full resolved spectrum; the sample factors and native modes contain the selected nconf columns.

docs.title: Optional observation modes and query projection
docs.text:
An optional mode_writer(first,last,modes) callback receives selected observation modes in a second pass. In Python its bounds are instead (start,stop) and half-open, as for the reader. The writer can store each block on disk without accumulating a full \(Q\times N\) array. info.observation_passes records whether the fitting call used one or two passes.

When observation modes are omitted, new observations are encoded using a cross-Gram product. For a query \(g=h-\bar h\),

\[ k=\frac{1}{S}H^\mathsf{T}Wg, \qquad x_j=\sqrt{\frac{S}{\lambda_j}}\,a_j^\mathsf{T}k. \]

transform_streaming rereads construction blocks and reconstructs their means; it always uses those means to center the queries. The construction reader and weights must be the same as in the fit. Encoding physical observations still requires those observations to be available for the query. Choosing reduced coordinates directly and applying the native backmap requires only the compact model.

docs.title: Storage and scope
docs.text:
The resident snapshot fit uses \(O(RS+S^2)\) working storage, plus the returned modes, with \(O(bS)\) temporary block storage. The direct fit instead uses the \(Q_+\times Q_+\) observation covariance. Neither solver builds a dense weight matrix.

The streamed native fit uses \(O(bS+S^2+MS+SN+MN)\) storage and retains no full observation array. A caller-supplied weight vector adds \(O(Q)\) storage; a weight reader avoids it. An optional mode writer determines where the \(Q\times N\) output is stored. Query encoding adds a \(T\times S\) cross-Gram matrix and blocks with at most \(bT\) entries. A large sample count remains expensive because the Gram matrix and its dense eigensolve still depend on \(S\).

The controlled manuscript driver in benchmarks/snapshot/verify_manuscript.py uses these public toolkit APIs for the prescribed spectrum, geometric regeneration, conditioning checks and a native-only run with 1,048,576 coordinates. Its saved outputs identify the actual source files, environment and input protocol; earlier results from separate research scripts are not silently relabelled as toolkit results.

See Reproducibility for the direct-reference tests and the comparison of current MATLAB and Python results.

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text:
PME-toolkit automatically generates visualization figures during the benchmark workflow.

These figures help interpret the dimensionality reduction results produced by PME, PI-PME, and PD-PME and evaluate the quality of the reduced representation.

The figures on this page illustrate the glider and airfoil benchmark outputs.

The normal MATLAB and Python case workflows generate plots in io.outdir. The Python runner also provides --no-plots to skip figures.

docs.title: Visualization workflow
docs.text:
Visualization figures are generated automatically when running a benchmark case.

After execution, the configured output directory contains the generated figures and report data. Relative output paths are interpreted from the case directory.

A typical results directory contains files such as:

results/
- report.mat
- scree_plot.png
- variance_retained.png
- variance_by_source.png
- nmse_by_source.png
- variable_modes_normalized.png
- mode_01.png
- mode_02.png
- mode_03.png

Model saving adds model.npz in Python or model.mat in MATLAB. The exact files depend on the configuration and available source blocks. In particular, PD-PME does not generate geometric-mode figures because its embedding excludes geometry.

direct, snapshot and auto use the same plotting functions and output names. The physical modes recovered by snapshot are used in the figures; the eigenvectors of the sample Gram matrix are not plotted as geometry.

docs.title: Eigenvalue spectrum (Scree plot)
docs.text:
The scree plot shows the eigenvalue spectrum associated with the embedding. Only the numerically resolved positive spectrum is returned and plotted.

A rapid decay of the eigenvalues indicates that most of the relevant variability of the design space can be captured using a small number of retained modes.

This plot is useful to assess:

  • intrinsic dimensionality of the design space
  • relative importance of successive modes
  • potential truncation levels for the reduced representation

docs.title: Retained variance
docs.text:
The cumulative retained variance indicates how much of the total variance of the embedding is captured by the retained modes.

Typical thresholds used in dimensionality reduction include:

  • 95% retained variance
  • 99% retained variance

The denominator is the full weighted trace before numerical-rank truncation. The selected dimension reaches the requested threshold while keeping the complete eigenvalue cluster at the boundary. When unresolved variance prevents the target from being reached, all resolved modes are retained and the achieved fraction is reported.

docs.title: Retained variance by information source
docs.text:
When multiple information sources are included in the embedding (for example geometry and physical quantities), it is useful to analyze how the retained variance is distributed across them.

This plot helps understand:

  • whether the embedding is mainly driven by geometry
  • whether physical observables contribute significantly
  • how balanced the reduced representation is across heterogeneous sources

This analysis is particularly relevant for PI-PME and PD-PME workflows.

docs.title: Reconstruction error by information source
docs.text:
The normalized mean squared reconstruction error (NMSE) can also be analyzed separately for each information source.

This plot indicates how accurately the reduced representation reconstructs each component of the dataset.

Lower NMSE values indicate better reconstruction accuracy. The global NMSE uses weighted residual energy with the same metric as fitting. Constant sources contribute no variance to the retained-variance curves.

This visualization is useful to compare reconstruction quality across heterogeneous data sources.

docs.title: Variable participation in retained modes
docs.text:
When design variables are included in the embedding, their contribution to the retained modes can be visualized.

This plot shows the normalized absolute contribution of each design variable to each retained mode.

It helps interpret the reduced coordinates and identify which original variables most strongly influence the latent representation.

docs.title: Geometric modes
docs.text:
The geometric interpretation of the reduced coordinates can be visualized through modal perturbations of the baseline geometry.

Example of first geometric mode of the PME embedding for the airfoil benchmark.

The mode perturbations use the baseline geometry and the geometric part of the recovered mode, with amplitude 3*sqrt(lambda). Reversing an eigenvector's sign exchanges the positive and negative curves. Repeated eigenvalues can admit different modal bases for the same subspace.

In this figure:

  • the black curve represents the baseline configuration
  • the blue curve represents the positive perturbation along the mode
  • the red curve represents the negative perturbation

This visualization provides an interpretation of how each reduced coordinate modifies the original geometry. For PD-PME, geometric reconstruction instead requires native backmapping and the user's geometry generator.

docs.title: Interpreting the visualizations
docs.text:
The different plots should be interpreted together to obtain a complete understanding of the reduction quality.

Important considerations include:

  • eigenvalue decay indicates intrinsic dimensionality
  • retained variance quantifies global information preservation
  • source-wise variance highlights the contribution of heterogeneous data
  • NMSE measures reconstruction accuracy
  • variable participation supports interpretability
  • geometric modes reveal deformation patterns associated with the reduced coordinates

Together, these visualizations support both quantitative evaluation and qualitative interpretation of the reduced design space.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
The exact appearance and number of generated figures depend on the selected benchmark configuration and the information sources included in the embedding.

Visualization is included in both language workflows. The advanced fit_streaming API returns a compact native model and does not automatically produce this standard plot set. Geometric plots from streamed fits require recovered observation modes and the corresponding geometry metadata; an optional mode writer can save those modes without retaining them all in memory.

For benchmark setup and execution, see the documentation pages on Benchmarks, Datasets, and Reproducibility.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
This page describes the standard PME-toolkit workflow from input data to outputs.

PME-toolkit is organized as a configuration-driven pipeline:

  1. define the input dataset
  2. define the workflow in a JSON configuration file
  3. run dimensionality reduction
  4. inspect results and visualizations
  5. optionally perform backmapping

docs.title: 1. Input dataset
docs.text:
A PME workflow starts from a dataset containing one or more of the following components:

  • geometry
  • design variables
  • physical information

These components must be sample-aligned, i.e. each sample must refer to the same design configuration across all data sources.

The dataset is typically stored in an external .mat file and referenced in the configuration through:

"io": {
  "dbfile": "path/to/database.mat"
}

See the Datasets and Input data pages for details.

docs.title: 2. JSON configuration
docs.text:
The workflow is fully defined through a JSON file.

A standard run configuration specifies:

  • method (mode)
  • eigensolver (solver: auto, direct or snapshot)
  • retained variance (CI)
  • geometry definition (geom)
  • design variables (vars)
  • physical quantities (phys, if applicable)
  • filters (filters)
  • input/output settings (io)

This JSON file is the central entry point of the workflow. Existing inputs may omit solver; both implementations then use auto. The distributed fitting examples declare it explicitly.

See the Configuration specification page.

docs.title: 3. Preprocessing
docs.text:
Before dimensionality reduction, the dataset may be filtered and normalized.

Available preprocessing steps include:

  • removal of samples containing nonfinite values
  • goal-oriented filtering
  • IQR-based filtering
  • variable-range handling

These operations are controlled in the filters and vars sections of the configuration file.

docs.title: 4. Dimensionality reduction
docs.text:
PME-toolkit supports three main modes:

  • pme → geometry + variables
  • pi → physics-informed reduction
  • pd → physics-driven reduction

The workflow constructs the embedding from the data described in the configuration and retains the number of modes required to satisfy the confidence index:

CI = retained variance threshold

Typical values are:

  • 0.95
  • 0.99

The result is a reduced latent representation of the original design space. The solver choice changes the eigensolve and mode recovery within this common workflow. direct solves the weighted covariance on positive-weight observation rows; snapshot solves the sample Gram matrix; auto chooses the smaller one. Both share the same numerical-rank cutoff and use the full weighted trace as the retained-variance denominator. The selection includes a complete repeated eigenvalue cluster at the confidence boundary. If the resolved spectrum cannot reach CI, the model reports the achieved fraction and emits a warning.

The standard case runner loads the full database into memory. Selecting snapshot does not switch the file loader to streaming. For observations read from disk or generated in blocks, use the streamed API.

docs.title: 5. Outputs
docs.text:
A standard run produces:

  • reduced coordinates
  • retained dimensionality
  • eigenvalues and modes
  • reconstruction metrics
  • saved model
  • visualization outputs

Results are typically written under:

results/

depending on the io.outdir setting. Relative paths in the fitting configuration are interpreted from the directory containing that configuration. Model files are model.npz in Python and model.mat in MATLAB; both workflows produce report.mat.

docs.title: 6. Visualization
docs.text:
Visualization is part of the standard workflow and helps interpret the quality of the embedding.

Typical outputs include:

  • scree plot
  • retained variance
  • variance by source
  • NMSE by source
  • variable participation
  • geometric modes

These plot families are shared by direct and resident snapshot fitting. PD-PME does not include a geometry block in its embedding and therefore does not produce geometric-mode plots. The compact streaming API requires an observation-mode writer and geometry metadata for corresponding mode plots.

See the Visualization page.

docs.title: 7. Backmapping
docs.text:
After a model has been generated, reduced coordinates can be mapped back to the original variable space through a separate backmapping workflow.

Backmapping requires:

  • the original case configuration
  • reduced coordinates input
  • a dedicated backmapping JSON file

The backmapping file does not need a solver setting: it uses the saved model.

Run it with:

docs.title: Python
docs.text: pme-back tests/cases/test_glider_back.json

docs.title: MATLAB
docs.text:
run_back("tests/cases/test_glider_back.json")

See the Backmapping and Backmapping configuration pages.

docs.title: Python
docs.text: pme-run tests/cases/test_glider.json

docs.title: MATLAB
docs.text:
run_pme("tests/cases/test_glider.json")

These commands execute the full workflow on the self-contained glider reference case.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The PME-toolkit workflow is:

  • data-driven
  • configuration-driven
  • reproducible
  • modular

The same logic applies to standard tests, benchmark cases, and externally hosted datasets.

docs.title: Regression on the Zenodo airfoil dataset
docs.text:
The release regression uses the complete RAE2822 airfoil benchmark from Zenodo record 18958555, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18958555. The database has 410 rows and 16,385 columns: 258 geometry coordinates, 20 native variables, 129 pressure coefficients and three scalar responses. No columns are subsampled for this regression.

The SHA256 of the extracted database.mat is:

a662f691c90158503ad627d1e4c36edafe566ec2fedb2ef3cadaacbb509cc177

The scripts verify both the checksum and the database shape before fitting. They use the existing benchmarks/standard/*/airfoil/case.json files and their configured filters. Removing columns with nonfinite data leaves 8,516 samples. PME uses these samples. The additional standard IQR filter leaves 7,391 samples for PI-PME and PD-PME. The baseline remains in each case.

docs.title: Comparisons
docs.text:
The unchanged pre-snapshot implementation is taken from commit 68309805. It runs in a separate package namespace in Python and a separate MATLAB process. The Python regression verifies its source files against that commit. The current version runs with each of solver="auto", solver="direct" and solver="snapshot". The complete filtered dataset is used even when the snapshot solver is explicitly selected.

Each comparison checks:

  • Identical filter masks, weights and retained dimension at CI=0.95.
  • Retained eigenvalues, and the resolved positive spectrum with errors scaled by the leading eigenvalue. Unresolved null modes are excluded from the spectral comparison.
  • Explained variance divided by the complete weighted trace.
  • Retained observation modes in the weighted norm, after sign alignment for isolated eigenvalues. Repeated eigenvalues are compared through their invariant subspace projector, since the individual eigenvectors may rotate.
  • Native-variable mode components and the reconstructed native training data.
  • An independent symmetric observation-covariance eigensolve, separate from both the original implementation and the current solver dispatch.

The eigenvector comparison concerns the retained basis used by the reduced model. It does not require eigenvectors associated with numerical null modes to agree. Native reconstruction is compared between implementations; this is not a claim that truncating at 95% observation variance recovers every native variable exactly.

The acceptance limits are 5e-9 for the maximum retained-eigenvalue relative error and the leading-eigenvalue-scaled spectrum error, 5e-7 for the weighted projector, sign-aligned retained modes and relative native-reconstruction errors, and 5e-10 for the absolute explained-variance difference.

docs.title: Recorded Python results
docs.text:
The initial full-dataset snapshot regression was run on candidate b36723d. The following values compare that snapshot implementation with the unchanged pre-snapshot implementation:

Method Samples retained by filters Retained modes Explained variance Maximum retained eigenvalue relative error Maximum sign-aligned weighted mode error PME 8,516 5 95.1777828647% 1.84e-15 5.05e-15 PI-PME 7,391 7 96.2809447954% 4.28e-15 2.76e-14 PD-PME 7,391 6 95.8627977450% 5.10e-15 2.14e-14

The resolved positive ranks were 126, 231 and 107, respectively. The maximum absolute difference over the resolved spectrum, divided by the leading eigenvalue, was 5.13e-16, 1.39e-15 and 3.42e-15. The absolute explained variance differences were at most 8.89e-16; relative native-reconstruction differences were at most 1.64e-14.

The subsequent local auto and direct runs also passed for all three methods, with identical retained dimensions and explained variances. The largest retained-eigenvalue relative error was 4.56e-15, and the largest weighted retained-mode error was 1.79e-14.

With two BLAS threads in the local environment, the three forced-snapshot fits took 74.2, 45.9 and 46.8 seconds. Direct fits took 0.16–0.36 seconds. These measurements describe this dataset and environment, not a general performance guarantee. There are many more retained samples than weighted observation rows, so auto chooses direct for this dataset. Snapshot is advantageous in the opposite regime.

docs.title: Reproduce and verify the release candidate
docs.text:
Create a checkout of the unchanged reference without modifying its files:

git worktree add --detach ../pme-legacy 68309805e9aff5a9b877c33982c7181d8faa550b
python -m pip install -e ./python
OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=2 OMP_NUM_THREADS=2 MKL_NUM_THREADS=2 \
  python tests/python/zenodo_snapshot_regression.py \
  --legacy-root ../pme-legacy \
  --output results/airfoil_regression.json

The script downloads the archived Zenodo database if necessary. Its JSON report records the repository commit, whether the source directory contains uncommitted changes, source-file checksums, dataset checksum, filter counts, spectra and numerical comparison errors. It does not store machine-specific input paths.

The Zenodo snapshot regression workflow runs the unchanged and current MATLAB implementations, then compares their outputs against both Python implementations. Its airfoil-regression artifact contains the JSON comparison report and both MATLAB output files. The workflow must pass on the final release candidate before merging. The local Python measurements above do not substitute for that MATLAB and cross-language gate.
